key_insight: A correct final diagnosis can conceal potentially harmful intermediate decisions, and correcting an error can introduce new risks.
clinical_relevance: Clinical AI evaluation should assess the safety of tests, treatments and disposition decisions throughout care—not just diagnostic accuracy.
method: Replayed admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, revealing only evidence available at each step.
Scored each decision separately for clinical validity and potential harm using an LLM judge calibrated against physician review.
Branched trajectories at the first actionable error to compare structured corrections with bare rejection.
evidence_signal: Across 300 cases from three sources, 55.2% of hospital trajectories reaching an acceptable diagnosis included moderate or severe potential harm; structured corrections resolved more first errors than bare rejection (73.6% vs 24.8%) but more often introduced new potentially unsafe decisions (30.2% vs 19.7%).
watch_item: These retrospective audits measured potential harm rather than observed patient injury, and physician calibration covered a stratified sample rather than every decision.
paper_title: Right Diagnosis, Unsafe Route: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories and Corrective Oversight for Validity and Potential Harm
